questions.prompt: Walk through Netgum's CheckoutService.CreateSessionAsync as a map of transaction boundaries: which work runs before the payment-gateway call and why it is placed there, what the single SaveChangesAsync at the end covers on SQL Server, which effect lies outside every transaction, and what a client that retries after a timeout ends up with.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Everything that can be decided locally is decided before the provider is called: the customer's name and email, the published product and variant, and the coupon's discount at one captured instant; nothing tracked has been changed yet, so a failure here leaves no trace anywhere.

[w3] The one SaveChangesAsync carries three tracked writes together: the new order row, the variant's lowered stock count and the coupon's raised redemption count; on SQL Server they land as a unit or not at all.
[w2] The InMemory provider used by the tests applies those changes without a transaction, so the suite cannot prove the all-or-nothing property; it proves ordering and call counts.
keyPoints.quote: InMemory applies them one by one with no rollback.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The payment intent is created at the provider during the await, before any database write, and no transaction can include it: if the post-await checks or the save fail, the intent exists at the provider and no code path cancels it.

[w2] Each call mints a fresh order id and therefore a fresh intent, so a client that retries after a timeout gets a second order, a second intent and a second unit of stock reserved; nothing in the request ties the retry to the first attempt.

[w1] The chapter lists what a production command would add instead of pretending the preflight is a transaction: idempotency keys, authorization, webhook signature checks, atomic stock constraints and an outbox.
keyPoints.quote: A future production command would need idempotency keys

questions.prompt: Defend or indict the post-await ValidatePurchase. Two buyers check out the last unit of a variant (StockQuantity = 1) at the same moment, each request in its own scoped DbContext against SQL Server. Trace both requests through the code as it is: what does the second ValidatePurchase actually read, what does each SaveChangesAsync write for the variant and for a limited coupon both buyers use, and how many orders and how much stock remain? Then say what would close the race.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The product is loaded once, before the gateway call, as a tracked aggregate with its variants and coupons included; that in-memory object is what every later check and mutation in the request works on.

[w3] The second ValidatePurchase runs on that same object and issues no query: it looks up the variant in the aggregate's own list, so a commit made by the other request during the await is invisible. Both requests still see a stock of 1 and both pass.

[w3] Each request then lowers its own copy from 1 to 0, and SaveChangesAsync writes the new value, not a decrement; the variant mapping has no concurrency token, so the second UPDATE is not rejected. Result: two orders, one unit sold twice, stored stock 0.

[w2] The coupon suffers the same lost update: both requests see a redemption count below the limit, both pass CanRedeem and both write count + 1, so a coupon with one redemption left is used twice and its stored count rises by one.

[w3] Closing it means letting the database decide at write time: make the stock change a conditional statement that only succeeds while stock is still positive and treat zero affected rows as sold out, or add a row-version token so a stale write fails and the request is rejected or retried.
keyPoints.quote: a conditional update the database evaluates

keyPoints.text: [w2] Whichever guard is chosen, a request that loses after the intent was created must cancel or abandon that intent, or the stock claim must happen before the provider is called; the guard alone fixes the oversell, not the stray intent.
[w1] The tests cannot show this race: they share one context and an in-memory provider, which tracks objects and accepts writes a relational database would arbitrate.
keyPoints.quote: EF InMemory tracks objects and accepts operations that a relational database may reject.

questions.prompt: Explain what CheckoutService.CompleteOrderAsync guarantees and what it does not: which repeated calls are safe and why, what its save covers, where the receipt email sits relative to the commit, and what happens when two completion requests for the same pending order arrive at the same time.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A repeat call on a terminal order is cheap and side-effect free: the failed case answers before any product read, and the paid case answers with the stored receipt before the provider is asked, anything is saved or any email is sent.

[w2] For a pending order the provider is asked for the intent's status; a failed status is one transition and one save, and a status that is neither failed nor succeeded throws without saving, so the caller can simply try again later.

[w3] The paid transition is committed first and the receipt is sent afterwards, outside the transaction: a crash between the two leaves a paid order whose buyer never got the email, and every later completion takes the early paid return and never sends it. Recording the email as an outbox row in the same save closes that gap.

[w3] Two simultaneous completions of a pending order both read Pending, both ask the provider, both mark the order paid and both save, because the order mapping carries no concurrency token; then both send a receipt. The early return only helps a caller who reads the order after another call has committed.
[w2] Making the transition a guarded write fixes that: with a row-version token the second save fails instead of silently repeating the change, so only the winner goes on to send the receipt.
[w2] The provider's intent id, which completion uses to find the order, carries a unique index, so the database itself guarantees that one intent can never be attached to two orders.
